title: Australian stick insects turn out to be five species, not two
summary:
How can a large, often photographed insect still surprise scientists? In Australia, some stick insects looked familiar, but their identities needed another careful check.

A University of Sydney team studied Australian insects in the group called Anchiale. Insects previously classified as two species turned out to represent five separate species. They live from northern New South Wales along coastal Queensland and into tropical northern Australia.

The team identified two previously unrecognized species and restored recognition of a third. One large insect had been incorrectly identified for decades. It is now recognized as its own species, Anchiale robusta.

The researchers gathered several kinds of clues. They studied DNA, the material that carries inherited information, alongside museum specimens, field surveys and insects raised in captivity. They also used observations shared by members of the public.

One newly described species, Anchiale mabiensis, lives in Queensland’s critically endangered Mabi rainforest. Its eggs have an unusual lid structure that had not previously been recorded in stick insects or their closest relatives.

Knowing which species is which can matter outside a museum. Some stick insects sometimes become so numerous that they strip leaves from trees. One insect associated with these outbreaks turned out to include more than one species. Telling them apart could help people understand effects on forests and farming.

The team also suspects another new species lives in Cape York. More specimens are needed before that possibility can be confirmed.
why_it_matters: Identifying species more accurately can reveal overlooked insect diversity and could help people understand effects on forests and farming.
